summary: Describes how to proxy UDP through HTTP, much as the HTTP CONNECT method proxies TCP. It defines a protocol letting an HTTP client create a tunnel for UDP traffic through an HTTP server acting as a proxy. It is a standards-track specification.

plainLanguage.summary: RFC 9298 defines a way for an HTTP client to ask a proxy to carry UDP traffic to a target. The client identifies the target in the request, and the proxy sends and receives UDP payloads for that tunnel.

subtitle: Defines how a client asks an HTTP proxy to carry UDP packets to a target.

tldr.problem: HTTP CONNECT tunnels TCP through a proxy, but does not by itself provide an equivalent way to proxy UDP traffic.
tldr.mechanism: A client sends a connect-udp request using a URI template that identifies the target host and port. The proxy opens a UDP socket and maps HTTP Datagrams to UDP payloads and back.
tldr.outcome: The mechanism works across HTTP versions and can carry UDP-based protocols such as QUIC. The RFC warns that proxies need controls to prevent abuse.

today: RFC 9298 is a Proposed Standard published in August 2022. It has been updated by RFC 9484 and RFC 9931.

sections.title: Proxying UDP through HTTP
sections.content:
HTTP CONNECT creates a TCP tunnel through a proxy. RFC 9298 defines a similar protocol for UDP, allowing an HTTP client to create a tunnel through a server acting as a UDP proxy. The tunnel can carry protocols that use UDP, including QUIC.

The client identifies the UDP proxy with an absolute URL and uses a URI Template to include the destination host and port. The protocol uses HTTP Datagrams and supports HTTP/1.x, HTTP/2 and HTTP/3.
sections.plainLanguage: An HTTP client can ask a proxy to send UDP packets to a specified target. The request carries the target address, and HTTP Datagrams carry the UDP payloads.

sections.title: Configuring the Target URI
sections.content:
The client's URI Template includes target_host and target_port. The host can be a DNS name, IPv4 literal or IPv6 literal. Colons in an IPv6 literal MUST be percent-encoded, and scoped zone identifiers are not supported.

The template must be absolute, include a non-empty scheme, authority and path, and use permitted template expansions. If a client detects an invalid template, it MUST reject the configuration and stop before sending a request. The RFC gives /.well-known/masque/udp/ as a default path prefix.
sections.plainLanguage: The template provides places for the target's host name or address and port. The client validates the template before using it and encodes colons in IPv6 addresses.

sections.title: Opening the UDP Tunnel
sections.content:
The client sends the connect-udp token. With HTTP/1.1, it uses GET with Connection and Upgrade headers and the proxy confirms success with status 101. With HTTP/2 or HTTP/3, it uses Extended CONNECT and a successful response has a 2xx status. The successful response also starts the Capsule Protocol.

The proxy resolves a DNS target before replying and rejects the request if resolution fails. Because UDP is connectionless, a proxy cannot know whether the target is reachable before it sends a packet. The proxy opens a UDP socket and keeps it open while the request stream remains open.
sections.plainLanguage: The client requests a connect-udp tunnel using the HTTP-version-specific request form. The proxy opens a UDP socket and reports success without first requiring a reply from the target.

sections.title: Context IDs and Datagram Payloads
sections.content:
Every HTTP Datagram associated with a UDP proxying stream starts with a variable-length Context ID. Context ID zero marks an ordinary UDP payload. Non-zero IDs are reserved for extensions; clients allocate even values and proxies allocate odd values.

With Context ID zero, the remaining bytes are the unmodified UDP payload and MUST NOT exceed 65527 bytes. A receiver that gets a larger payload MUST abort the stream. A datagram with an unknown Context ID can be dropped or buffered temporarily; receivers that buffer SHOULD set limits to reduce resource exhaustion.
sections.plainLanguage: Each datagram starts with a context number. Zero means the remaining data is a UDP payload, which can be at most 65527 bytes.

sections.title: Packet Size and Congestion Behavior
sections.content:
A UDP proxy MUST NOT introduce IP fragmentation when forwarding datagrams. It silently drops oversized datagrams and, in IPv4, sets the Don't Fragment bit when possible. For HTTP/3 DATAGRAM frames, an outgoing UDP payload that cannot fit SHOULD be dropped, with an ICMP Packet Too Big message sent to the target.

Proxies SHOULD avoid increasing traffic burstiness and SHOULD NOT queue packets merely to batch them. Since proxied traffic may run nested congestion controllers, the HTTP connection MUST NOT disable congestion control without certainty that the inner traffic is controlled. UDP proxying SHOULD use HTTP/3 when the inner protocol uses loss recovery.
sections.plainLanguage: The proxy drops packets that cannot fit instead of fragmenting them. It should avoid batching traffic into bursts and must preserve congestion control unless it knows the inner traffic is controlled.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
A proxy that allows any client to reach any UDP target can be used to send traffic attributed to the proxy. The RFC says servers should restrict UDP proxy use to authenticated users.

Proxies should also prevent access to vulnerable targets, such as their own addresses and localhost, link-local, multicast or broadcast addresses. UDP does not have shared connection state with the target, so a proxy may continue sending during some denial-of-service attacks even when the target is unable to respond.
sections.plainLanguage: An unrestricted UDP proxy can hide the sender's address and reach sensitive targets. The RFC recommends authentication and blocking targets that could let a client gain unintended access.
